body: In general, the legal regime of the Arctic is based on (fragmented) international law and the domestic law of the Arctic-8 states (Drumbl & Uhlířová 2021). These legal systems and specific rules intersect and interact, making Arctic governance complex and multifaceted (Schönfeldt 2020). This is clear in the context of the 1920 Svalbard Treaty, which recognises Norway’s sovereignty over the archipelago while allowing commercial activities (including mining or fishing) by other treaty parties, based on the principle of non-discrimination of foreigners. Despite this, Norway is not willing to treat citizens of other treaty parties equally with regard to operations on the continental shelf around Svalbard, as became evident in a dispute regarding fishing for snow crab on the seabed. In this context, Norway claims exclusive rights over the continental shelf surrounding Svalbard on the basis of UNCLOS, which grants the coastal state the right to treat its own nationals preferentially (Oystein 2020). Other states argue that Norway’s regulation of waters beyond its territorial sea should be subject to the Svalbard Treaty, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of nationality in relation to certain activities, giving foreigners equal rights to hunting, fishing and mining in Svalbard and its territorial seas (Article 2 Svalbard Treaty). The rules of the UNCLOS and Svalbard Treaty are thus perceived as contradictory. Fishing for snow crabs by Latvia and other EU member states in this area has contributed to an ongoing legal and diplomatic dispute between Norway, the EU and other parties to the Svalbard Treaty7 on the status of waters surrounding Svalbard and on fishing rights. These disputes culminated in confrontational actions, such as Norway’s 2017 detention of the Latvian vessel Senator, which was operating on the Norwegian continental shelf without a permit from the Norwegian authorities. Not willing to risk straining the EU’s bilateral relations with Norway, the European Commission sought solutions based on dialogue and a constructive approach, regardless of how much time this would take (European Commission 2020, par. 53, 54). Recently, Russia has been increasing its presence in Svalbard within the terms of the Svalbard Treaty (Nilsen 2021; McVicar 2022).

Indeed, in 2021, Russia filed a submission to the UN CLCS to extend its claim to the Arctic Ocean seabed, which overlaps with those of Canada and Denmark. Russian claims currently cover around 70% of the Arctic Ocean seabed (Breum 2021). In 2023, the UN CLCS actually approved most of Russia’s claim while Denmark and Canada still have their claims unresolved (Hager 2023). While this move could potentially increase tensions between Russia and other Arctic states, as long as the process follows UNCLOS provisions the states involved might be ‘amenable to the expansion’ (Kuras 2021).

In addition to the above examples of peaceful resolution of territorial disputes and treaty observance, cooperative actions are further supported by a ‘complex network of institutionalised relations’ (Chrášťanský & Kříž 2011) and coalition-building. The soft-law regime of the Arctic Council (AC) has been described as ‘the most comprehensive international body in the Arctic region’ (Byers 2013). Institutionally, the AC, International Maritime Organisation and Barents Euro-Arctic Co-operation have an especially important role in resolving specific issues. The Declaration on the Establishment of the Arctic Council of 1996 explicitly stated that it would promote cooperative activities while not dealing with matters related to military security (Arctic Council 1996). Global geopolitical issues and power competition were therefore excluded in this leading inter-governmental forum even during conflicts such as Russia’s illegal use of force in Crimea in 2014, when Russia de facto annexed Crimea and faced international sanctions (Byers 2017; Dodds & Woon 2020). However, Russian actions outside the Arctic can affect relations with other Arctic states, a clear example being Russia’s 2022 military aggression against Ukraine, which has ‘substantially affected’ Russian relations with Norway, the US and Canada, and introduced elements of heightened competition and tension into the Arctic’s geopolitical environment.8 There have been various treaty-like cooperative initiatives, such as the 2018 US–Russia scheme for managing two-way shipping traffic through the Bering Sea and the 2020 US and Russia Joint Contingency Plan for combating maritime pollution.9 Nonetheless, increased tensions and competition are apparent, for example, due to the NATO exercises Trident Juncture 18, held in 2018, and Cold Response, held in 2022, with a total of about 30,000 soldiers, marines and airmen from 27 countries participating (NATO 2022a).

In the last decade, the AC has become ‘the focal point for treaty-making’ in the Arctic (Koivurova 2014). In 2011, the AC members adopted a search-and-rescue treaty (Arctic Council 2011a) as a first legally binding instrument under the auspices of the AC (Byers 2017). A second binding instrument on cooperation on marine-oil pollution preparedness and response was signed at the Kiruna Ministerial Meeting in 2013 (Arctic Council 2013), while a third legally binding agreement, negotiated under the auspices of the AC and signed in 2017, aimed to enhance international Arctic scientific cooperation (Arctic Council 2017). All AC observers10 affirm (Arctic Council 2011b, p. 50) the primacy of the Arctic-8 states’ sovereignty and jurisdiction in the Arctic (Rainwater 2015). Lastly, the 2013 admission of China as an observer in the AC means that all five UN Security Council permanent members are now either members or observers of the AC (Charron 2014).

Despite their divergent interests, the Arctic-8 countries are united in their resistance to any attempts by non-Arctic countries (such as Germany or France) to interfere with their division of the Arctic (Olesen 2017), as also illustrated by the Ilulissat Declaration of 2008, a joint regional effort in response to the effects of climate change. The Ilulissat Declaration was brought by the coastal states of the Arctic Ocean (the United States, the Russian Federation, Canada, Norway and Denmark), which claim to be in ‘a unique position to address these possibilities and challenges’ (2008 Ilulissat Declaration).
